Photosynthesis. The fundamental biochemical process by which plants, algae, and some bacteria convert light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose. Occurring primarily in leaf chloroplasts, it consumes carbon dioxide and water to produce carbohydrates and oxygen. Photosynthesis is the foundation of nearly all food chains and the primary source of atmospheric oxygen, making it essential to life on Earth.

The light-dependent reactions occur in the thylakoid membrane of chloroplasts. They capture photons via chlorophyll and other pigments. Water molecules are split through photolysis to release molecular oxygen as a byproduct, along with electrons and protons. These reactions generate ATP and NADPH, high-energy molecules that power the next stage of photosynthesis. The reactions are organized into two photosystems, Photosystem II and Photosystem I, which work in series.

The Calvin cycle, also called the light-independent reactions, occurs in the stroma. It uses ATP and NADPH from the light reactions to fix carbon dioxide. This is catalyzed by Rubisco, or RuBP carboxylase, the most abundant enzyme on Earth. Rubisco binds carbon dioxide to ribulose-one-five-bisphosphate and produces three-phosphoglycerate, which is reduced to glyceraldehyde-three-phosphate. Most of this G3P is recycled to regenerate RuBP; the remainder exits the cycle to build glucose.

The overall equation is six CO2 plus six H2O plus light yields one glucose plus six O2. Light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration, and temperature all limit the rate of photosynthesis. C3 plants, which include most crops, are less efficient than C4 and CAM plants in arid conditions due to photorespiration, where Rubisco's tendency is to oxygenate RuBP instead of carboxylating it.

Photosynthesis emerged roughly two point five billion years ago with cyanobacteria and transformed Earth's atmosphere from oxygen-free to oxygen-rich. It is responsible for nearly all biomass production; animals are heterotrophs entirely dependent on photosynthetic energy capture. Photosynthesis is a cornerstone of ecology and evolution, and understanding its two-stage structure—light-dependent and light-independent—is key to discussing chloroplast biology, metabolism, and the deep history of life.
